neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented to person and place; knows the month and year but cannot state the exact date or day of the week. MMSE 21/30, losing points on recall (0/3 at 5 minutes), orientation (3 points lost), attention/calculation (2 errors on serial sevens). Clock drawing test shows numbers clustered on the right side of the clock face with hands placed at an incorrect time. Unable to recall any of 3 words after 5 minutes, even with categorical cues. Naming intact for common objects but hesitates for less frequent items. Repetition intact. Comprehension intact for simple instructions but has difficulty following a three-step command. Fluency mildly reduced for category naming.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal, round, and reactive to light. Extraocular movements full without nystagmus. Visual fields full to confrontation. Facial sensation intact. Face symmetric with normal strength. Hearing grossly intact bilaterally. Palate elevates symmetrically. Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius strength 5/5 bilaterally. Tongue midline without fasciculations or atrophy.
neurological_exam.motor: Bulk and tone normal throughout all extremities. No rigidity, no bradykinesia, no resting or postural tremor. Strength 5/5 in all extremities. No pronator drift.
neurological_exam.sensory: Intact to light touch, pinprick, vibration, and proprioception in all extremities. Mildly decreased vibration sense at bilateral great toes, attributed to age.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ and symmetric at biceps, triceps, brachioradialis, patellar, and Achilles bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally. No Hoffmann sign. No Babinski sign.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose testing intact bilaterally without dysmetria. Heel-to-shin testing normal. Rapid alternating movements intact. No past-pointing.
neurological_exam.gait: Steady gait with normal base and stride length. Tandem gait intact. Romberg sign negative. No ataxia. Turns normally without instability.
neurological_exam.additional: No paratonic rigidity. No grasp reflex. No myoclonus. No signs of parkinsonism. Orthostatic vital signs: supine BP 138/78, standing BP 130/74 at 3 minutes — no significant orthostatic drop.

patient.chief_complaint: Progressive memory loss and difficulty managing daily activities over the past two years
patient.history_present_illness: Mrs. Yumi Tanaka is a 73-year-old right-handed retired seamstress who presents to the outpatient neurology clinic accompanied by her daughter, Akiko, for evaluation of worsening memory difficulties over the past two years. The daughter first noticed subtle changes approximately two years ago when her mother began repeating questions during their weekly phone calls, sometimes asking the same question three or four times within a single conversation without apparent awareness of having done so. Over the following months, additional concerns emerged. Mrs. Tanaka, who had been an accomplished seamstress for decades, began making errors in sewing patterns she had known by heart for years, producing garments with misaligned seams and incorrect measurements. She also started having difficulty managing her household finances, a task she had handled independently for the entirety of her marriage. Her husband discovered several unpaid utility bills and noticed that the checkbook register contained arithmetic errors, which was highly unusual for her. Approximately one year ago, Mrs. Tanaka got lost walking home from the local market, a route she had taken daily for over twenty years, and had to call her daughter for directions. Since then, she has been reluctant to walk alone and prefers to stay in the apartment. She has forgotten to take her medications on multiple occasions, prompting her daughter to set up a pill organizer. Her cooking has also been affected; she has burned meals several times after forgetting she had left the stove on, and her husband now supervises all cooking activities. The daughter notes that her mother seems less interested in activities she previously enjoyed, including watching her favorite television programs and tending to her small balcony garden. Mrs. Tanaka acknowledges that her memory is not as good as it used to be and appears distressed about the changes, occasionally becoming tearful when discussing them. There have been no episodes of visual hallucinations, personality changes, or aggressive behavior. She has not experienced any falls, tremor, difficulty walking, seizures, or sudden onset neurological symptoms. Her sleep has been unremarkable according to her husband, with no reports of acting out dreams or excessive daytime somnolence. Three years ago, she experienced episodic dizziness upon standing that was evaluated and attributed to her antihypertensive medication; the amlodipine dose was reduced from 10 mg to 5 mg with resolution of symptoms. This prior orthostatic complaint has not recurred.

clinical_assessment.impression: Cognitive impairment documented on a validated bedside instrument with an amnestic-predominant profile, and delayed recall that does not recover with cueing — a storage rather than a retrieval deficit, which is the pattern of Alzheimer pathology. The informant history and the loss of instrumental independence establish decline from a previous level and place the syndrome at the dementia rather than the mild threshold. This assessment is the step that makes the syndrome measurable; imaging and biomarkers then attribute it.

Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test - Delayed Recall

output.impression: Neuropsychological evaluation demonstrates a predominantly amnestic profile with multi-domain involvement. Episodic memory is severely impaired: RAVLT delayed recall at the 1st percentile and immediate recall at the 3rd percentile, consistent with a storage-type encoding deficit. Semantic fluency (Category Fluency — Animals, 8th percentile) and confrontation naming (Boston Naming Test, 20th percentile) are below expected norms. Executive function (Trail Making B, 15th percentile) is mildly reduced. Processing speed (Trail Making A, 28th percentile) and visuoconstructive ability (Rey Complex Figure Copy, 30th percentile) are within low-normal range. Screening scores: MMSE 21/30, MoCA 16/30. Mood screening is borderline (GDS 5/15); cognitive deficits are disproportionate to any mood contribution. Profile is consistent with amnestic mild cognitive impairment, multi-domain type

interactions: No significant interactions with amlodipine, metformin, rosuvastatin, or alendronate
warnings: May cause bradycardia; baseline HR 72 bpm — monitor heart rate, particularly in combination with amlodipine
GI side effects (nausea, diarrhea, anorexia) are common at initiation, usually transient; monitor in context of concurrent metformin which may also cause GI symptoms
Avoid concurrent use of anticholinergic medications as they may reduce donepezil efficacy
alternatives: Rivastigmine (patch or oral) — alternative cholinesterase inhibitor, may have fewer GI side effects with transdermal formulation

results.title: 2023 AAN Practice Guideline: Mild Cognitive Impairment and Early Alzheimer Disease
results.summary: Recommends cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine) as first-line for mild-to-moderate AD. Memantine may be added at moderate stage. Anti-amyloid therapies (lecanemab, donanemab) may be considered for early AD with confirmed amyloid pathology in appropriate candidates.

results.title: Appropriate use recommendations for lecanemab and donanemab in Alzheimer disease
results.summary: Anti-amyloid antibodies require confirmed amyloid positivity (PET or CSF), MCI or mild dementia stage, APOE genotyping (e4 homozygotes at higher ARIA risk), baseline MRI screening for microbleeds. Require regular MRI monitoring for ARIA.

results.title: Non-pharmacological interventions in early Alzheimer disease
results.summary: Evidence supports cognitive stimulation therapy, physical exercise programs, occupational therapy, and caregiver education. Combined pharmacological and non-pharmacological approaches yield best outcomes.

output.summary: Cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine) have demonstrated symptomatic benefit in randomized controlled trials of early Alzheimer's disease. Anti-amyloid antibodies (lecanemab, donanemab) have demonstrated slowing of clinical decline in biomarker-confirmed early-stage populations; appropriate use criteria include confirmed amyloid pathology, MCI or mild dementia stage, and MRI screening for ARIA risk factors. Non-pharmacological interventions including cognitive stimulation and exercise show benefit in long-term follow-up studies.

differential.key_features: DLB must be actively excluded by absence of visual hallucinations, parkinsonism, cognitive fluctuations, and REM sleep behavior disorder; biomarkers and (when needed) DaTscan can distinguish if features emerge
FTD typically presents with prominent personality change, disinhibition, or progressive aphasia rather than amnesia; positive amyloid biomarkers further argue against FTLD pathology
No significant cerebrovascular burden on MRI and the gradual amnestic course is not stepwise — pure VCI is unlikely
Insidious course over months to years with disproportionate delayed-recall impairment and limited benefit from cueing is not typical of pseudodementia

differential.diagnosis: Reversible metabolic, endocrine, or sleep-related cognitive impairment
differential.key_features: Screening labs exclude hypothyroidism, B12 deficiency, neurosyphilis, and HIV; the progressive amnestic profile would not normalize with treatment of any of these alone

optimal_actions.action: Obtain detailed clinical history from patient and informant, including timeline, cognitive domains affected, functional decline, mood, sleep, and medication review
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Gradually progressive cognitive change with informant-confirmed functional impairment in IADLs

optimal_actions.action: Perform bedside cognitive assessment (MMSE and/or MoCA) and detailed neurological examination
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Objective cognitive impairment on MoCA more sensitive than MMSE; non-focal neurological exam (or variant-specific findings — visuospatial in PCA, language in lvPPA, behavioral in frontal AD)

optimal_actions.action: Order reversible-cause labs (CBC, CMP, TSH, vitamin B12, folate; consider RPR/HIV per risk)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Reversible mimics (hypothyroidism, B12 deficiency, neurosyphilis) excluded; identify and address co-morbid metabolic factors

optimal_actions.action: Obtain brain MRI with dementia (volumetric) protocol to assess medial-temporal atrophy and exclude vascular disease, hippocampal sclerosis, NPH, and mass lesions
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Bilateral medial-temporal / hippocampal atrophy (Scheltens MTA grade 2-3) with temporoparietal cortical volume loss

optimal_actions.action: Order comprehensive neuropsychological testing to characterize the cognitive profile and establish a baseline for tracking
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Amnestic profile with disproportionate impairment of delayed recall and limited benefit from cueing, plus involvement of at least one other cognitive domain

optimal_actions.action: Order CSF biomarkers (Aβ42, Aβ42/40 ratio, p-tau, total tau) for ATN classification
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Reduced Aβ42 (or reduced Aβ42/40 ratio) with elevated p-tau supporting A+T+ profile consistent with Alzheimer pathology

optimal_actions.action: Order amyloid PET when CSF biomarkers are unavailable or when diagnostic uncertainty persists after clinical assessment and MRI
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Positive cortical amyloid retention (SUVr above positivity threshold) confirming amyloid pathology

optimal_actions.action: Order FDG-PET to assess regional metabolism and distinguish AD from frontotemporal dementia or other neurodegenerative patterns
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Bilateral temporoparietal and posterior cingulate hypometabolism characteristic of Alzheimer pattern

optimal_actions.action: Check drug interactions before initiating cholinesterase inhibitor (donepezil, rivastigmine, or galantamine)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: No clinically significant interactions; counsel on GI side effects and bradycardia risk

optimal_actions.action: Perform a structured cognitive and behavioural assessment with informant history: a validated bedside instrument with the per-domain breakdown, whether delayed recall improves with cueing, and an explicit account of which instrumental activities have been lost. The syndrome must be documented before it is attributed
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Impairment documented on a validated instrument with an amnestic-predominant profile and informant-confirmed decline from a previous level, staged by whether independence in instrumental activities is preserved (mild cognitive impairment) or lost (dementia)

optimal_actions.action: Disclose the diagnosis to patient and family, discuss prognosis, advance directives, and driving / safety assessment
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Patient and caregiver engaged in care planning; safety concerns (driving, finances, medication management) addressed

useless_tools.rationale: ECG is unrelated to the dementia workup; no cardiac symptom or syncope to justify it in this case
Echocardiography is unrelated to the dementia workup; no cardioembolic indication in this presentation
Cardiac monitoring is not indicated; no arrhythmia, syncope, or palpitations described
Head CT adds little when MRI is available; MRI is the preferred structural modality for dementia workup

sequence_constraints.reason: Obtain structural imaging before lumbar puncture to exclude mass effect / herniation risk, particularly in older patients

critical_actions: Obtain collateral history from an informant who knows the patient well
Exclude reversible causes of cognitive decline with screening labs (CBC, CMP, TSH, B12, folate; HIV/RPR per risk)
Obtain structural brain MRI with dementia/volumetric protocol
Quantify cognitive impairment with a standardized cognitive battery (MoCA at minimum; formal neuropsychological testing when feasible)
Assess safety: driving, medication management, finances, and need for caregiver support
Disclose the diagnosis and discuss prognosis, advance directives, and treatment options with the patient and family
Pursue biomarker confirmation (CSF AT(N) markers or amyloid PET) when MRI is equivocal or when an atypical AD variant is suspected
contraindicated_actions: Do not prescribe anticholinergic medications (e.g., diphenhydramine, oxybutynin, tricyclics) which worsen cognition in patients with AD
Do not prescribe benzodiazepines as first-line management of anxiety or insomnia given fall and cognitive risk
Do not start antipsychotics without a clear behavioral indication given the FDA boxed warning for increased mortality in dementia
Do not attribute symptoms entirely to normal aging, depression, or sleep apnea without completing the dementia workup
Do not start memantine monotherapy at the mild stage (memantine is approved for moderate-to-severe AD)
key_reasoning_points: Definite hippocampal and temporoparietal atrophy on MRI with a multi-domain amnestic cognitive profile is sufficient to make a clinical diagnosis of probable AD by NIA-AA 2011 criteria
The hallmark cognitive feature of AD is impaired delayed recall with rapid forgetting and limited benefit from cueing, reflecting a storage-type (hippocampal) memory deficit
APOE genotyping is a risk modifier and is not used to make the diagnosis; an E3/E4 or E4/E4 result is supportive but neither sufficient nor required for diagnosis
Low-normal B12 should prompt methylmalonic acid testing before being dismissed as a non-contributor
Cholinesterase inhibitors are first-line symptomatic therapy in mild-to-moderate AD; memantine is reserved for moderate-to-severe disease

metadata.difficulty_description: Straightforward case with classic amnestic presentation, supportive family history, characteristic MRI findings of hippocampal atrophy, and absence of features suggesting alternative diagnoses. The clinical picture clearly points to Alzheimer disease with minimal confounders.
metadata.adaptation_notes: Clinical foundation inspired by published MSA case. Patient demographics modified to fit typical AD presentation (age increased to 73, cerebellar/autonomic features replaced with progressive amnestic syndrome). The source case's orthostatic dizziness is preserved as a historical finding attributed to medication, and the normal posterior fossa structures on MRI explicitly exclude MSA.
